html:
This is one of the two heavyweight inorganic chapters — about 4 questions — and it is unashamedly factual: preparations, properties, tests and which reagent does what to whom. The winning strategy is to file each species under three hooks — how it is made, what kind of agent it is (oxidant, reductant, acid, dehydrator…), and its one diagnostic test — and to know the trends that bind families (halogen reactivity falls down the group, HX acidity rises). Every equation below is balanced; in the examination hall, write the same way: charge and atoms both counted.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Hydrogen: nascent [H] (freshly generated, e.g. Zn + HCl) reduces more strongly than molecular H₂; atomic H from an electric arc is fiercer still (atomic hydrogen torch). Isotopes: ¹H (protium), ²H/D (deuterium), ³H/T (tritium, β⁻, t½ 12.3 y). D₂O (heavy water): denser (1.106 g cm⁻³), b.p. 101.4 °C — a neutron moderator and tracer.
  • Oxides: acidic (CO₂, SO₂, NO₂), basic (Na₂O, CaO), amphoteric (Al₂O₃, ZnO), neutral (CO, NO, N₂O, H₂O), peroxides (Na₂O₂: O at −1), superoxides (KO₂: −½), mixed (Fe₃O₄, Pb₃O₄).
  • Ozone: 3O₂ ⇌ 2O₃ by silent electric discharge; bent (116.8°), resonance-equal bonds, strong oxidant (starch–iodide turns blue; Hg loses its meniscus — "tailing of mercury"). CFC chlorine radicals catalytically destroy stratospheric O₃ → UV shield thinning (Montreal Protocol 1987).
  • NH₃: Haber (450 °C, 200 atm, Fe/Mo); pyramidal lone-pair base & ligand ([Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ deep blue); Nessler's test (brown). PH₃: Ca₃P₂ + water; rotten-fish, poisonous, far less basic/soluble than NH₃.
  • HNO₃: Ostwald (NH₃/Pt gauze → NO → NO₂ → absorb); oxidizing acid — Cu + dil. → NO, Cu + conc. → NO₂; Fe/Al go passive in conc. HNO₃; aqua regia (1 HNO₃ : 3 HCl) dissolves Au/Pt; brown-ring test for NO₃⁻.
  • Halogens: reactivity F > Cl > Br > I; colours pale-green/red-brown/violet; each higher halogen displaces lower halides. HX acidity HF ≪ HCl < HBr < HI; reducing power runs the other way; HF etches glass (→ SiF₄).
  • Carbon: diamond (sp³, hardest, insulator), graphite (sp² layers, conductor, lubricant), fullerene C₆₀, graphene. CO: from formic acid + conc. H₂SO₄; neutral oxide, strong reductant, binds haemoglobin ~250× O₂ (poison); water gas = CO + H₂, producer gas = CO + N₂.
  • H₂S: FeS + dil. H₂SO₄ (Kipp); rotten eggs, weak dibasic acid, reductant; blackens lead-acetate paper; the group-analysis precipitant (Ch. 22). SO₂: acidic oxide, reducing bleach (temporary!), turns acidified dichromate green. H₂SO₄: Contact process (V₂O₅, oleum), dehydrating + oxidizing (hot conc.) — "king of chemicals".

13.1 Atomic, molecular and nascent hydrogen; isotopes; heavy water; types of oxides

Ordinary hydrogen is the molecular diatomic gas. Two more reactive forms are exam staples: nascent hydrogen [H], the just-born atoms liberated in situ by a reaction such as Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + 2[H], which reduce things (e.g. acidified KMnO₄, Fe³⁺ salts, KClO₃) that bubbling molecular H₂ through the same solution leaves untouched; and atomic hydrogen, made by passing H₂ through an electric arc — its atoms recombine on a surface releasing so much heat (≈ 4000 °C, the atomic hydrogen torch for welding refractory metals) and it is the strongest reducing form of all: reducing power: atomic H > nascent [H] > molecular H₂. (Modern chemistry treats "nascent" effects as adsorbed hydrogen atoms/electron transfer at the metal surface — the exam keeps the classical name and ranking.)

Isotope Nucleus Abundance/behaviour Uses
Protium ¹H 1 p 99.985 % —
Deuterium ²H (D) 1 p + 1 n 0.015 %; stable D₂O, tracers, NMR solvents, fusion fuel
Tritium ³H (T) 1 p + 2 n radioactive β⁻, t½ 12.3 y luminous signs, biological labelling (Ch. 12)

Heavy water, D₂O, is obtained in practice by prolonged electrolysis of ordinary water (containing alkali) — H₂ is evolved preferentially, concentrating D₂O behind — or by the Girdler-sulfide exchange industrially. Its molecules are heavier, so its constants crawl up (m.p. 3.8 °C, b.p. 101.4 °C, density 1.106 g cm⁻³, maximum density at 11.6 °C) and its reactions run slower; organisms tolerate only dilution (high fractions are toxic because enzyme kinetics and mitotic spindles depend on those very rates). Its headline job is the neutron moderator in CANDU-type reactors, where its low neutron absorption lets natural (unenriched) uranium burn.

Types of oxides (memory scheme: the partner's character decides):

Type Examples Behaviour/test
Acidic (mostly non-metals, high oxidation states) CO₂, SO₂, SO₃, NO₂, P₂O₅, CrO₃ turn moist litmus red; +base → salt + water; many are acid anhydrides
Basic (metals) Na₂O, CaO, MgO, CuO +acid → salt + water
Amphoteric Al₂O₃, ZnO, PbO, SnO react with both acid and alkali
Neutral CO, NO, N₂O, H₂O neither acidic nor basic to litmus
Peroxides (O = −1) Na₂O₂, BaO₂, H₂O₂ give H₂O₂ with dilute acid
Superoxides (O = −½) KO₂, RbO₂ large alkali metals in excess O₂; used to regenerate O₂ in spacecraft/submarines
Mixed Fe₃O₄ (FeO·Fe₂O₃), Pb₃O₄ (2PbO·PbO₂) two formal oxides in one lattice

Volumes of ozone and oxygen

Problem. 90 mL of oxygen is converted to ozone in a silent discharge, and the conversion reaches 60 % by volume of oxygen consumed. Later the ozone fully decomposes. What volumes of ozone form and of oxygen return? Solution. Ozonisation runs 3O₂ → 2O₃: 60 % of 90 mL = 54 mL of O₂ reacts, giving 2/3 × 54 = 36 mL of O₃ (with 36 mL O₂ left over, 72 mL total gas). Decomposition runs 2O₃ → 3O₂: 36 mL of O₃ returns 3/2 × 36 = 54 mL of O₂, restoring the original 90 mL. Volume arithmetic of gases is stoichiometry at constant T and P — Gay-Lussac doing the counting.

13.2 Ozone: preparation, structure and tests; depletion of the ozone layer

Preparation. A slow, silent (sparkless) electric discharge through dry oxygen in an ozonizer (Siemens/Brodie) gives up to ~10 % of the pale-blue, pungent gas:

3O₂ ⇌ 2O₃ (ΔH = +285 kJ — endothermic; heat destroys the product, hence the silent, cold discharge)

Pure ozone is condensed out as a deep-blue, dangerously explosive liquid. Structure: the molecule is bent (bond angle 116.8°, O–O 127 pm — between single (148) and double (121)), a resonance hybrid of two forms with an sp² central oxygen carrying a lone pair; the delocalized π system makes both bonds equal (bond order 1.5). Properties: a powerful oxidant — stronger than O₂, because it sheds an atom of "nascent oxygen", O₃ → O₂ + [O]: it oxidizes I⁻ to I₂ (starch–iodide paper turns blue — the standard test), black PbS to white PbSO₄, and mercury suffers tailing (oxidized to Hg₂O, it loses its meniscus and sticks to glass — the classic distinguishing test); it bleaches dyes and disinfects drinking water without chlorine's taste. Its quantity is estimated iodometrically (O₃ + 2KI + H₂O → I₂ + O₂ + 2KOH).

The ozone layer (stratosphere, 20–35 km) absorbs 97–99 % of the Sun's medium UV (200–315 nm), shielding DNA from its mutagen. Depletion: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs — old refrigerants/aerosols) survive to that altitude, where UV frees chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone:

Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, and ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂ (the Cl• is regenerated: one atom kills ≈ 10⁵ O₃ molecules)

with the Antarctic spring "ozone hole" worsened by polar stratospheric clouds. The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased CFCs out worldwide — atmospheric chlorine is falling and the layer is on a slow (mid-century) mend, the most successful environmental treaty to date; NO from jets and N₂O are also catalytic offenders. Consequences of thinning: more UV-B → skin cancer, cataracts, phytoplankton and crop damage. (Do not confuse good stratospheric ozone with bad ground-level ozone, a photochemical-smog pollutant — Ch. 21.)

13.3 Ammonia, phosphine and nitric acid

Ammonia NH₃. Laboratory: heat NH₄Cl with slaked lime, 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃↑ + 2H₂O, and dry over quicklime (never conc. H₂SO₄ or CaCl₂ — both absorb it). Industrial: Haber, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at 450 °C, 200 atm, Fe/Mo (Ch. 7's compromise). A colourless, pungent gas, fantastically soluble in water (the fountain experiment: ~700 volumes in 1), giving the weak base NH₄OH. Its trigonal- pyramidal molecule (sp³ N, lone pair at the apex) explains both faces: it is a base (turns litmus blue; dense white fumes of NH₄Cl with HCl vapour — a field test), and a ligand, donating the pair to metal ions: pale-blue Cu(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NH₃ to the deep-blue tetraammine [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ (Schweizer's reagent chemistry, Ch. 14). Tests: Nessler's reagent (alkaline K₂[HgI₄]) gives a brown colour/precipitate with even traces of NH₃/NH₄⁺. Uses: fertilizers (urea, ammonium salts), HNO₃ manufacture, refrigeration, and (aqueous) as a laboratory base and complexing agent.

Phosphine PH₃. From calcium phosphide and water, Ca₃P₂ + 6H₂O → 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2PH₃↑ (companion: white phosphorus boiled with NaOH gives PH₃ + sodium hypophosphite). A colourless, rotten-fish/garlic-smelling, very poisonous gas, sparingly soluble, only feebly basic (PH₄⁺ salts form only with strong acids like HI; basicity NH₃ ≫ PH₃ because the lone pair sits in a diffuse 3s-ish orbital on the bigger atom) and a stronger reductant than NH₃. Impure PH₃ (with P₂H₄ vapour) ignites spontaneously in air — the basis of Holmes' signals (sea flares: Ca₃P₂ + CaC₂ cannisters) and of marsh "will-o'-the-wisp" tales.

Nitric acid HNO₃. Laboratory: distil KNO₃/NaNO₃ with conc. H₂SO₄ in an all-glass retort (KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃↑). Industrial: Ostwald's process — 4NH₃ + 5O₂ →(Pt–Rh gauze, ~800 °C) 4NO + 6H₂O; 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; 2NO₂ + H₂O → HNO₃ + HNO₂ (practically 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO, the NO recycled). Pure HNO₃ is colourless but commercial acid is yellow-brown from dissolved NO₂ (made by its photodecomposition — store shaded). It is both a strong acid and a fierce oxidizing agent whose reduction product tracks concentration:

Reaction Product gas Notes
Cu + dilute HNO₃: 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO↑ + 4H₂O NO (browns in air) the standard equation
Cu + conc. HNO₃: Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂↑ + 2H₂O NO₂ (brown)
Zn + very dilute/cold HNO₃ even NH₄NO₃ (N reduced to −3) deeper reduction with active metals
Fe, Al, Cr + conc. HNO₃ no attack — passivity dense oxide film; hence conc. HNO₃ ships in aluminium
Non-metals + hot conc.: C → CO₂, S → H₂SO₄, P → H₃PO₄, I₂ → HIO₃ — HNO₃ plays pure oxidant
Aqua regia: HNO₃ + 3HCl (1 : 3) dissolves Au, Pt nascent Cl₂ and NOCl do the work

Test: the brown ring — FeSO₄ solution + conc. H₂SO₄ down the side gives a brown ring of [Fe(NO)]SO₄ at the junction (NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻ confirm; Ch. 22).

13.4 Chlorine, bromine and iodine; HCl, HBr and HI

The group-17 elements are diatomic, coloured, and hangrier for electrons at the top: oxidizing power F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂, so the higher halogen displaces the lower from its salts (Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂; Br₂ will not displace Cl⁻ in return). Laboratory Cl₂: warm MnO₂ with conc. HCl (MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂↑ + 2H₂O, similarly KMnO₄ acts in the cold); industry gets it from brine electrolysis (Ch. 10) and historically by Deacon's 4HCl + O₂ → 2Cl₂ + 2H₂O (over CuCl₂ catalyst). Chlorine water bleaches by oxidation (via HOCl) and its bleaching is permanent (contrast SO₂ below); with cold dilute NaOH it gives NaCl + NaClO (bleach liquor), with hot concentrated, NaCl + NaClO₃; over slaked lime it makes bleaching powder, Ca(OCl)Cl. Bromine (red-brown fuming liquid) is won from sea-water/brines by chlorine displacement; iodine (violet vapour, sublimes, starch turns deep blue) from seaweed ash and Chilean nitrate deposits; both dissolve in KI solution (as I₃⁻) and in organic solvents with characteristic colours (Br₂ orange in CCl₄; I₂ violet in CCl₄, brown in water/ethanol — a living qualitative test).

Hydrogen halides are made by displacing from salts with a non-volatile acid — with a crucial exception:

HX Preparation Acid strength in water Signature
HF CaF₂ + conc. H₂SO₄ (in lead/Pt, not glass!) weak (strong H–F bond, H-bonding) etches glass: SiO₂ + 4HF → SiF₄↑ + 2H₂O — used for marking glassware, fluoridation
HCl NaCl + conc. H₂SO₄; direct synthesis H₂ + Cl₂ (industry) strong white fumes with NH₃; AgCl white ppt, soluble in NH₄OH
HBr not conc. H₂SO₄ (it oxidizes HBr → Br₂); use H₃PO₄, or PBr₃ + water stronger reducing agent
HI H₃PO₄ route or PI₃ hydrolysis; conc. H₂SO₄ would give I₂ strongest strongest reductant of the four; even reduces conc. H₂SO₄ to H₂S/S

Trends in one breath: bond strength HF > HCl > HBr > HI, so thermal stability falls and acidity and reducing power rise down the group; silver halide tests run AgCl (white, NH₄OH-soluble) → AgBr (pale yellow, sparingly soluble) → AgI (yellow, insoluble) as Ksp falls (Ch. 7 patterns again).

13.5 Allotropes of carbon and carbon monoxide; H₂S, SO₂ and sulphuric acid

Allotropes. Diamond: every C sp³-bonded in a 3-D tetrahedral lattice — the hardest natural substance, electrical insulator, superb heat conductor, transparent, very high melting. Graphite: sp² sheets (each C bonded to three, the fourth electron delocalized) held by weak forces — soft, slippery (pencil "lead", lubricant), conducts electricity along the planes (electrodes, brushes). Fullerenes (C₆₀ buckminsterfullerene, soccer-ball cages), graphene (a single graphite sheet — Physics Ch. 22), nanotubes, and the amorphous family (coke, charcoal — adsorptive, gas masks; lampblack/carbon black — inks, tyres). Whichever the costume, the chemistry (combustion to CO₂ 393.5 kJ per mole for graphite) is carbon's.

Carbon monoxide CO. Laboratory: dehydrate formic (or oxalic) acid with hot conc. H₂SO₄: HCOOH → CO↑ + H₂O. Industrial: producer gas (air over red-hot coke: CO + N₂) and water gas (steam over coke: CO + H₂, endothermic — alternated with air blasts). Colourless, odourless, almost insidiously poisonous: it binds haemoglobin (carboxyhaemoglobin) some 200–250 times more avidly than O₂ — faulty room heaters kill silently, and cherry-red blood is the post-mortem clue. Chemically a neutral oxide (yet it reduces Fe₂O₃ in the blast furnace, Ch. 14), burns with a blue flame (2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂), and is a strong ligand (Ni + 4CO ⇌ Ni(CO)₄, the Mond refining step).

Hydrogen sulphide H₂S. Kipp's apparatus, FeS + dil. H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂S↑ (never conc. acid or HNO₃ — they oxidize it). Rotten-egg gas, denser than air, very poisonous (and treacherously paralyses the sense of smell). A weak dibasic acid (→ HS⁻ → S²⁻) and a reductant (decolorizes Br₂ water and acidified KMnO₄, depositing sulfur). Its kingdom is analysis: with controlled [S²⁻] (acidic vs alkaline medium, the common-ion machinery of Ch. 7) it precipitates metal sulphides group by group (Ch. 22). Test: lead acetate paper turns black (PbS).

Sulphur dioxide SO₂. Made by burning sulfur, roasting sulphides (4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂), or Cu + hot conc. H₂SO₄. Pungent, denser than air, very soluble; an acidic oxide (H₂SO₃ in water; salts sulphites/bisulphites) — a major acid-rain precursor. It is a reducing agent (turns acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ paper green, Cr³⁺ — its distinguishing test; decolorizes KMnO₄) and its bleaching, by reduction of coloured matter to colourless, is temporary (air slowly re-oxidizes the fabric — the eternal pair with chlorine's permanent oxidative bleach).

Sulphuric acid H₂SO₄ — the "king of chemicals". Contact process: purify SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ over V₂O₅ at ~450 °C and modest pressure (exothermic: low T favoured but rate demands compromise, Ch. 7); absorb SO₃ not in water (violent mist) but in conc. H₂SO₄ to give oleum H₂S₂O₇, then dilute to order. Properties to file in threes: (1) strong dibasic acid (first proton complete); (2) dehydrating agent when concentrated — chars sugar to black carbon (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O), dries gases (not NH₃, HBr, H₂S), and demands respect on dilution — always acid into water, the mixing is fiercely exothermic; (3) oxidizing agent when hot and concentrated (Cu + 2H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + SO₂↑ + 2H₂O; C → CO₂ + SO₂). Tests: BaCl₂ gives a white precipitate of BaSO₄ insoluble in acids. Industrial fingerprints: fertilizers ((NH₄)₂SO₄, superphosphate), detergents, petroleum refining, lead-acid batteries (density of the acid even gauges their charge, Ch. 10).

Worked example 13.1 — identify the gas

Problem. A colourless gas G (i) turns limewater milky slowly, (ii) turns acidified potassium dichromate solution green, (iii) decolorizes bromine water, and (iv) bleaches a coloured flower, whose colour returns in a few days. Identify G and the chemistry of (ii).

Solution. G is SO₂: a reducing, acidic gas with temporary reductive bleaching (CO₂ would fail (ii)–(iv); Cl₂'s bleaching is permanent and it is greenish). (ii) SO₂ reduces orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ to green Cr³⁺: K₂Cr₂O₇ + H₂SO₄ + 3SO₂ → K₂SO₄ + Cr₂(SO₄)₃ + H₂O (Cr +6 → +3; S +4 → +6).

The three not-with-conc.-H₂SO₄ cases

Concentrated sulphuric acid fails as a maker/drier whenever the other partner reduces it or is a base: HBr and HI (oxidized to Br₂, I₂), H₂S (oxidized to S), NH₃ (acid–base). Examiners ask for the workarounds (H₃PO₄ for HBr/HI; CaO to dry NH₃; dil. acid for H₂S).

Common mistake

Six swaps the paper sets: nascent hydrogen is atomic hydrogen in statu nascendi, not a different element; D₂O moderates neutrons but poisons eukaryotic life in bulk — the same property list; chlorine bleaches by oxidation (permanent), SO₂ by reduction (temporary); aqua regia is 3 HCl : 1 HNO₃, not the reverse; HF is weak despite fluorine's electronegativity, because the H–F bond and hydrogen bonding hold the proton; and SO₃ is absorbed into acid as oleum, never into water, which would fog it into an unusable mist.

Disproportionation of chlorine in cold vs hot alkali

Problem. Write the balanced ionic equations and oxidation-state changes when \text{Cl}_2 reacts with (a) cold, dilute \text{NaOH} and (b) hot, concentrated \text{NaOH}.

Solution. (a) Cold dilute alkali gives chloride (-1) and hypochlorite (+1): \text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}^- + \text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}. (b) Hot concentrated alkali disproportionates \text{Cl}_2 (0) into chloride (-1) and chlorate (+5) in a 5 : 1 molar ratio: 3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{OH}^- \rightarrow 5\text{Cl}^- + \text{ClO}_3^- + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}.

Chapter summary

  • Hydrogen's personas scale in reducing violence (H₂ < [H] < atomic H); its isotopes give heavy water (a moderator) and tritium (a tracer).
  • Oxides sort by character — acidic, basic, amphoteric, neutral, peroxide, superoxide, mixed — and ozone is oxygen's bent, resonating, oxidizing allotrope, whose stratospheric veil CFC chemistry taught us to defend.
  • Ammonia is base and ligand in one lone pair; phosphine its feebler, fouler sibling; nitric acid an oxidizing acid whose product gas advertises its concentration.
  • Halogens weaken downwards as oxidants while their hydrides strengthen as acids and reductants; HF alone is weak — and alone eats glass.
  • Carbon reinvents itself from diamond to graphene; CO poisons quietly and refines metals; the sulphur trio H₂S/SO₂/H₂SO₄ escalates from analytical precipitant to the dehydrating, oxidizing king of chemicals.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (d) — atoms not yet paired into H₂ (and surface-adsorbed H) reduce directly; molecular H₂ must first break its bond.

2. (a) — deuterium oxide; tritium water would be T₂O (a biohazard, option (c) is a real but different thing).

3. (c) — mass 3 with the lone charge of hydrogen.

4. (b) — CO is neutral (also NO, N₂O, H₂O). (a), (c) acidic; (d) basic.

5. (a) — dual behaviour with acids and alkalis.

6. (d) — sparkless discharge: the product is endothermic and easily destroyed by heat/sparks.

Three catalyst–process pairs never to scramble

Haber NH₃ = Fe/Mo; Ostwald HNO₃ = Pt–Rh gauze; Contact H₂SO₄ = V₂O₅. The options in at least one question a year are exactly these three, shuffled.
